b36l-tyler-4e91d638-t19.candidateText:
A few things beyond the route swap, since the new routes are estimates and ramp-up risk is real.

First, phase it. Don't exit Lakeport and Port Avery cold — the new routes may take months to build demand. Keep some defensive frequency where it at least covers variable cost while ramping Ashford and Brookhaven, so there's no revenue gap in the transition.

Second, pull the ancillary lever. Extras are only $20 per passenger across all routes. Raising bag, seat, and co-brand card revenue by even $10 per passenger across the whole network — on roughly 800,000 passengers a year — is real money and doesn't depend on fares.

Third, attack the cost gap directly. The competitor is 30% cheaper per seat partly on larger aircraft; Larkspur could look at crew productivity, maintenance, or renegotiating airport fees to lower that $9,000-ish variable cost per flight.

Fourth, protect the four healthy routes — they're the profit base; make sure nothing invites a low-cost entrant there.

I'd sequence these so year-one profit doesn't hinge entirely on the new-route estimates hitting.

b36l-tyler-4e91d638-t21.candidateText:
Let me quickly sanity-check that passenger figure before I recommend. Across six routes, 14,000 flights × 80 seats × roughly 75% load ≈ 840,000. So about 800,000 to 840,000 — fine.

My recommendation: Larkspur should exit the two routes where a lower-cost competitor has triggered an unwinnable price war and redeploy those aircraft to the two uncontested new routes. That alone swings the airline from a $4 million operating loss to roughly a $7.8 million operating profit within the year.

The logic: the entire $24 million profit swing came from Lakeport and Port Avery, where Larkspur now sells seats below variable cost. It can't out-price a competitor with 30% lower costs. Redeploying 5,000 flights to Ashford and Brookhaven generates about $10 million of new contribution against unchanged fixed costs.

Risks: the new-route fares and load factors are planning estimates — if demand disappoints, profit erodes; and a competitor could follow onto those routes. So I'd phase the exit, layer in higher ancillary revenue of $10-plus per passenger across ~800,000 fliers, and attack the cost gap in parallel.

Next step: stress-test demand on the two new routes before committing aircraft.
